page: Vultr vx1-m-32c-256g-1920s is a memory-optimized server instance within the VX1 Cloud Compute family. It features an x86_64 AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz, configured with 32 dedicated vCPUs derived from 16 physical cores with multithreading. The hardware configuration includes 256.0 GB of system memory, providing a memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. Storage is bundled as a local 1920 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU hardware is present.

Performance benchmarks indicate strong memory subsystem capabilities. The instance achieved top-tier status in large-block memory write bandwidth at 193.78 GB/sec and a top-tier Passmark memory score of 2989.67. Single-core performance is strong, with stress-ng single-core scoring 3055.98 and single-threaded gzip compression reaching 40.79 GB/sec. However, multi-core raw compute presents a relative tradeoff, with stress-ng multi-core performance scoring 48974.13, placing it in the average tier.

This server is configured for memory-intensive and storage-heavy workloads, such as database hosting, Redis caching, and large-scale data processing. Passmark database operations scored 22098.23, and Redis SET operations reached 63.9 million operations per second, confirming its efficiency for transactional systems. The high density of memory and local NVMe storage relative to the dedicated AMD EPYC vCPUs offers a cost-efficient profile for workloads requiring substantial RAM caching and fast local I/O without the need for GPU accelerators.
description: Vultr vx1-m-32c-256g-1920s is a memory-optimized server from the VX1 Cloud Compute family, powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC processor. It delivers 32 dedicated vCPUs across 16 physical cores, 256.0 GB of RAM, and a bundled 1920 GB NVMe SSD. Benchmark results highlight top-tier memory write bandwidth of 193.78 GB/sec and strong database performance, with Redis SET operations reaching 63.9 million operations per second. While single-core performance is strong, multi-core raw compute is average, representing a tradeoff for highly parallel CPU-bound tasks. This instance is cost-efficient for memory-intensive databases, caching layers, and high-throughput web serving.
